claim: Ferrous iron accumulates over adult lifetime in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Ferrous iron accumulates over adult lifetime in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing age-related increases in ferrous iron through X-ray fluorescence microscopy and φXANES spectroscopy.

claim: Glutathione depletion is coupled to ferrous iron elevation in aging C. elegans.
source: Here, we show that glutathione depletion is coupled to ferrous iron elevation in these animals, and that both occur in late life to prime cells for ferroptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing glutathione levels decrease with age while ferrous iron increases, and that SIH treatment prevents age-dependent glutathione decrease.

claim: Blocking ferroptosis by inhibition of lipid peroxidation mitigates age-related cell death.
source: We demonstrate that blocking ferroptosis, either by inhibition of lipid peroxidation or by limiting iron retention, mitigates age-related cell death and markedly increases lifespan and healthspan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that liproxstatin treatment reduces propidium iodide-positive dying cells and extends lifespan.

claim: Blocking ferroptosis by limiting iron retention mitigates age-related cell death.
source: We demonstrate that blocking ferroptosis, either by inhibition of lipid peroxidation or by limiting iron retention, mitigates age-related cell death and markedly increases lifespan and healthspan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that SIH treatment reduces propidium iodide-positive dying cells and extends lifespan.

claim: Blocking ferroptosis markedly increases lifespan in C. elegans.
source: We demonstrate that blocking ferroptosis, either by inhibition of lipid peroxidation or by limiting iron retention, mitigates age-related cell death and markedly increases lifespan and healthspan.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data showing approximately 70% median lifespan extension with Lip-1 and 100% with SIH.

claim: Blocking ferroptosis markedly increases healthspan in C. elegans.
source: We demonstrate that blocking ferroptosis, either by inhibition of lipid peroxidation or by limiting iron retention, mitigates age-related cell death and markedly increases lifespan and healthspan.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing improved movement parameters (maximum velocity, distance traveled) in aged animals treated with Lip-1 or SIH.

claim: Temporal scaling of lifespan is not evident when ferroptosis is inhibited.
source: Temporal scaling of lifespan is not evident when ferroptosis is inhibited, consistent with this cell death process acting at specific life phases to induce organismal frailty, rather than contributing to a constant aging rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using accelerated failure time models showing that lifespan increases by Lip-1 and SIH do not conform to temporal scaling (p<0.01).

claim: Ferroptosis acts at specific life phases to induce organismal frailty rather than contributing to a constant aging rate.
source: Temporal scaling of lifespan is not evident when ferroptosis is inhibited, consistent with this cell death process acting at specific life phases to induce organismal frailty, rather than contributing to a constant aging rate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal scaling analysis and hazard rate plots showing distinct effects of Lip-1 and SIH at different life stages.

claim: Excess age-related iron elevation in somatic tissue contributes to degenerative disease.
source: Because excess age-related iron elevation in somatic tissue, particularly in brain, is thought to contribute to degenerative disease, post-developmental interventions to limit ferroptosis may promote healthy aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on iron accumulation in aging and disease.

claim: Post-developmental interventions to limit ferroptosis may promote healthy aging.
source: Because excess age-related iron elevation in somatic tissue, particularly in brain, is thought to contribute to degenerative disease, post-developmental interventions to limit ferroptosis may promote healthy aging.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the experimental findings in C. elegans and the known role of iron in degenerative diseases.

claim: Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death program genetically and biochemically distinct from apoptosis, necrosis and autophagic cell death.
source: Ferrous iron drives ferroptosis, a regulated cell death program genetically and biochemically distinct from apoptosis, necrosis and autophagic cell death (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dixon et al., 2012.

claim: Ferroptosis kills malignant cells.
source: Ferroptosis kills malignant cells but may also be inappropriately activated in ischemic injury and neurodegeneration (Stockwell et al., 2017; Tuo et al., 2017; Viswanathan et al., 2017; Yang and Stockwell, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ferroptosis may be inappropriately activated in ischemic injury and neurodegeneration.
source: Ferroptosis kills malignant cells but may also be inappropriately activated in ischemic injury and neurodegeneration (Stockwell et al., 2017; Tuo et al., 2017; Viswanathan et al., 2017; Yang and Stockwell, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ferroptosis is executed by (phospho)lipid hydroperoxides induced by iron-dependent lipoxygenases.
source: This cell death mechanism is executed by (phospho)lipid hydroperoxides induced by either iron-dependent lipoxygenases, or by an iron-catalyzed spontaneous peroxyl radical-mediated chain reaction (autoxidation).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of ferroptosis mechanisms.

claim: Ferroptosis is executed by (phospho)lipid hydroperoxides induced by an iron-catalyzed spontaneous peroxyl radical-mediated chain reaction (autoxidation).
source: This cell death mechanism is executed by (phospho)lipid hydroperoxides induced by either iron-dependent lipoxygenases, or by an iron-catalyzed spontaneous peroxyl radical-mediated chain reaction (autoxidation).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of ferroptosis mechanisms.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions the ferroptotic signal is terminated by glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPx4).
source: Under homeostatic conditions the ferroptotic signal is terminated by glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPx4), a phospholipid hydroperoxidase that needs glutathione as a cofactor.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of GPx4 function in ferroptosis.

claim: GPx4 is a phospholipid hydroperoxidase that needs glutathione as a cofactor.
source: Under homeostatic conditions the ferroptotic signal is terminated by glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPx4), a phospholipid hydroperoxidase that needs glutathione as a cofactor.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of GPx4 biochemistry.

claim: The role of iron load in ferroptosis is poorly resolved.
source: While the signaling that regulates ferroptosis has been studied in depth (Conrad et al., 2016; Doll et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2015), the role of iron load in this death signal is poorly resolved (Doll and Conrad, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doll and Conrad, 2017.

claim: In C. elegans the emergence of labile ferrous iron with age correlates with genetic effects that accelerate aging.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans the emergence of labile ferrous iron with age correlates with genetic effects that accelerate aging (James et al., 2016; James et al., 2015) and could be a lifespan hazard (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to James et al., 2016 and James et al., 2015.

claim: Labile ferrous iron could be a lifespan hazard in C. elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans the emergence of labile ferrous iron with age correlates with genetic effects that accelerate aging (James et al., 2016; James et al., 2015) and could be a lifespan hazard (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2010.

claim: Excess iron supply shortens lifespan in C. elegans.
source: Excess iron supply has been shown to shorten lifespan in C. elegans (Gourley et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2008), yet variable results have been reported with iron chelation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gourley et al., 2003 and Hu et al., 2008.

claim: The iron chelator deferiprone was reported not to impact C. elegans lifespan.
source: The iron chelator deferiprone was reported not to impact C. elegans lifespan (Valentini et al., 2012), but this study was limited by indirect measures of iron load, use of only a single dose of deferiprone, and small sample size.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Valentini et al., 2012.

claim: CaEDTA caused a minor increase in C. elegans lifespan.
source: In contrast, use of calcium-ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (CaEDTA), a non-specific chelator that does not redox-silence iron, caused a minor (undisclosed) increase in lifespan (Klang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klang et al., 2014.

claim: The load of tissue iron increases needlessly in aging nematodes, mammals and humans.
source: The load of tissue iron increases needlessly in aging nematodes, mammals and humans (James et al., 2015; Massie et al., 1983; Massie et al., 1985; Ward et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies across different species.

claim: Fe2+-glutathione complexes are thought to be the dominant form of iron in the cellular labile iron pool.
source: This must tax regulatory systems that prevent abnormal redox cycling of iron, such as the Fe2+-glutathione complexes thought to be the dominant form of iron in the cellular labile iron pool (Berndt and Lillig, 2017; Hider and Kong, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berndt and Lillig, 2017 and Hider and Kong, 2011.

claim: Glutathione is the dominant coordinating ligand for cytosolic ferrous iron.
source: Glutathione is suggested to be the dominant coordinating ligand for cytosolic ferrous iron (Hider and Kong, 2011) and is also the substrate used by glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPX4) to clear the lipid peroxides that induce ferroptotic cell death (Dixon and Stockwell, 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hider and Kong, 2011.

claim: Glutathione is the substrate used by GPX4 to clear lipid peroxides that induce ferroptotic cell death.
source: Glutathione is suggested to be the dominant coordinating ligand for cytosolic ferrous iron (Hider and Kong, 2011) and is also the substrate used by glutathione peroxidase-4 (GPX4) to clear the lipid peroxides that induce ferroptotic cell death (Dixon and Stockwell, 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dixon and Stockwell, 2014; Friedmann Angeli et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Deletion of four C. elegans homologs of GPX4 decreases lifespan.
source: Deletion of four C. elegans homologs of GPX4 decreases lifespan (Sakamoto et al., 2014), but whether ferroptosis mediates this is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sakamoto et al., 2014.

claim: DEM at 10-100 µM increases lifespan via hormesis in C. elegans.
source: DEM has been reported to produce a non-linear response to glutathione depletion, with a minor glutathione loss induced by DEM at 10–100 µM increasing lifespan via hormesis, but a major glutathione loss induced by DEM ≥1 mM shortening lifespan (Urban et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Urban et al., 2017.

claim: DEM ≥1 mM shortens lifespan in C. elegans.
source: DEM has been reported to produce a non-linear response to glutathione depletion, with a minor glutathione loss induced by DEM at 10–100 µM increasing lifespan via hormesis, but a major glutathione loss induced by DEM ≥1 mM shortening lifespan (Urban et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Urban et al., 2017.

claim: DEM ≥1 mM induced death in 4 day old adult worms in a dose- and time-dependent manner.
source: We found that DEM ≥1 mM induced death in 4 day old adult worms (at the end of their reproductive phase) in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with ≈50% lethality occurring after 24 hr exposure to 10 mM DEM (Figure 1A) associated with ≈50% depletion of glutathione (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: 24 hr exposure to 10 mM DEM causes approximately 50% lethality in 4 day old adult worms.
source: We found that DEM ≥1 mM induced death in 4 day old adult worms (at the end of their reproductive phase) in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with ≈50% lethality occurring after 24 hr exposure to 10 mM DEM (Figure 1A) associated with ≈50% depletion of glutathione (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 24 hr exposure to 10 mM DEM is associated with approximately 50% depletion of glutathione in 4 day old adult worms.
source: We found that DEM ≥1 mM induced death in 4 day old adult worms (at the end of their reproductive phase) in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with ≈50% lethality occurring after 24 hr exposure to 10 mM DEM (Figure 1A) associated with ≈50% depletion of glutathione (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Total glutathione levels steadily decrease with normal aging in C. elegans, approaching approximately 50% on Day 10 of the levels on Day 1.
source: We also found that total glutathione levels steadily decrease with normal aging, approaching ≈50% on Day 10 of the levels on Day 1 (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: C. elegans become disproportionately more vulnerable to DEM lethality as they enter the midlife stage.
source: This may contribute to C. elegans becoming disproportionately more vulnerable to DEM lethality as they enter the midlife stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing age-dependent increase in DEM sensitivity shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both Lip-1 and SIH protect against lethality from DEM-derived glutathione depletion.
source: DEM toxicity in 4-day-old worms was rescued by both Lip-1 and SIH (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1), with more marked protection by SIH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: SIH provides more marked protection against DEM toxicity than Lip-1.
source: DEM toxicity in 4-day-old worms was rescued by both Lip-1 and SIH (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1), with more marked protection by SIH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ferroptosis contributes to the death mechanism induced by DEM in C. elegans.
source: This is consistent with ferroptosis contributing to the death mechanism.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue of DEM toxicity by ferroptosis inhibitors Lip-1 and SIH.

claim: The age-dependent rise in iron contributes to the fall in glutathione.
source: We found that this age-dependent rise in iron itself may contribute to the fall in glutathione, since pretreatment of the worms with SIH from L4 prevented the age-dependent decrease in glutathione when assayed on Day 4 of adult life (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing SIH prevents age-dependent glutathione decrease, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SIH pretreatment from L4 prevents the age-dependent decrease in glutathione when assayed on Day 4 of adult life.
source: We found that this age-dependent rise in iron itself may contribute to the fall in glutathione, since pretreatment of the worms with SIH from L4 prevented the age-dependent decrease in glutathione when assayed on Day 4 of adult life (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SIH mitigates the glutathione depletion induced by DEM in Day 4 animals.
source: Furthermore, SIH mitigated the glutathione depletion induced by DEM in Day four animals (Figure 1F), demonstrating that cytosolic iron synergizes the depletion of glutathione initiated by DEM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cytosolic iron synergizes the depletion of glutathione initiated by DEM.
source: Furthermore, SIH mitigated the glutathione depletion induced by DEM in Day four animals (Figure 1F), demonstrating that cytosolic iron synergizes the depletion of glutathione initiated by DEM.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that SIH (which chelates iron) prevents DEM-induced glutathione depletion.

claim: Lip-1 does not prevent the fall in glutathione induced by aging or by DEM.
source: While Lip-1 alleviated the lethality of DEM (Figure 1E), it did not prevent the fall in glutathione that was induced by aging (as assayed on Day 4) or by DEM (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Lip-1 inhibition of ferroptosis in C. elegans occurs downstream of glutathione depletion.
source: Thus, Lip-1 inhibition of ferroptosis in C. elegans occurs downstream of glutathione depletion, consistent with its effect in rescuing ferroptosis in cultured cells (Shah et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Lip-1 rescues DEM lethality without preventing glutathione depletion, and is supported by citation to Shah et al., 2018.

claim: A feature of ferroptosis is the propagation of cell death in a paracrine manner mediated by uncertain signals that might include 4-HNE and MDA.
source: A feature of ferroptosis is the propagation of cell death in a paracrine manner mediated by uncertain signals that might include the toxic lipid peroxidation end-products 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) and malondialdehyde (MDA) (Feng and Stockwell, 2018; Linkermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feng and Stockwell, 2018 and Linkermann et al., 2014.

claim: Cell death (particularly death of intestinal cells) precedes organismal death in 4-day-old adults.
source: Examination of aged cohorts, or young animals treated with DEM, indicated that cell death (particularly death of intestinal cells) preceded organismal death in both 4-day-old (Figure 2B) and 6- and 8-day-old (Figure 2C) adults, and was significantly attenuated by both Lip-1 or SIH.
evidence: This claim is supported by propidium iodide staining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cell death (particularly death of intestinal cells) precedes organismal death in 6- and 8-day-old adults.
source: Examination of aged cohorts, or young animals treated with DEM, indicated that cell death (particularly death of intestinal cells) preceded organismal death in both 4-day-old (Figure 2B) and 6- and 8-day-old (Figure 2C) adults, and was significantly attenuated by both Lip-1 or SIH.
evidence: This claim is supported by propidium iodide staining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cell death preceding organismal death is significantly attenuated by both Lip-1 and SIH.
source: Examination of aged cohorts, or young animals treated with DEM, indicated that cell death (particularly death of intestinal cells) preceded organismal death in both 4-day-old (Figure 2B) and 6- and 8-day-old (Figure 2C) adults, and was significantly attenuated by both Lip-1 or SIH.
evidence: This claim is supported by propidium iodide staining data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Death of individual cells prior to organismal death is consistent with progressive degeneration contributing to the frailty phenotype.
source: Death of individual cells prior to organismal death is consistent with progressive degeneration contributing to the frailty phenotype.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of cell death preceding organismal death.

claim: Acute glutathione depletion by 20 mM DEM exposure for 6 hr increases MDA levels in C. elegans.
source: As expected, acute glutathione depletion by DEM exposure caused a marked increase in the relative amounts of MDA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TBARS assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: An age-related increase in MDA occurs in C. elegans.
source: We also observed an aged-related increase in MDA, consistent with an age-related increase in ferroptotic signalling in C. elegans, that was ameliorated by both Lip-1 and SIH treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TBARS assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The age-related increase in MDA is ameliorated by both Lip-1 and SIH treatment.
source: We also observed an aged-related increase in MDA, consistent with an age-related increase in ferroptotic signalling in C. elegans, that was ameliorated by both Lip-1 and SIH treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TBARS assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 4-HNE protein adducts increase with age in C. elegans.
source: Consistent with the MDA results, we also found a concomitant qualitative increase in 4-HNE protein adducts with age that was suppressed by both Lip-1 and SIH treatments (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The age-related increase in 4-HNE protein adducts is suppressed by both Lip-1 and SIH treatments.
source: Consistent with the MDA results, we also found a concomitant qualitative increase in 4-HNE protein adducts with age that was suppressed by both Lip-1 and SIH treatments (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Neither 250 µM SIH nor 200 µM Lip-1 induces DAF-16 nuclear translocation.
source: Neither 250 µM SIH nor 200 µM Lip-1 induced DAF-16 nuclear translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by DAF-16::GFP localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with 10 mM DEM induces nuclear localization of DAF-16.
source: As a positive control, treatment with 10 mM DEM did induce nuclear localization of DAF-16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with this challenge inducing acute stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by DAF-16::GFP localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both total iron and areal density increase with age in control animals.
source: Both total iron and areal density increased with age in control animals (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary file 2), as expected (James et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and 3C, and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: SIH dramatically reduces the areal density of iron with aging.
source: SIH dramatically reduced the areal density of iron (and reduced variance) with aging (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 2), but Lip-1 did not alter iron density.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Lip-1 does not alter iron density.
source: SIH dramatically reduced the areal density of iron (and reduced variance) with aging (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 2), but Lip-1 did not alter iron density.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: By Day 8, animals treated with SIH contain total iron load on par with the untreated control group.
source: Notably, by Day 8, animals treated with SIH contained total iron load on par with the untreated control group (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 2), as the lower areal density was offset by an increase in body size of SIH-treated worms compared to age matched controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The lower areal density of iron in SIH-treated worms is offset by an increase in body size compared to age matched controls.
source: Notably, by Day 8, animals treated with SIH contained total iron load on par with the untreated control group (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 2), as the lower areal density was offset by an increase in body size of SIH-treated worms compared to age matched controls.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that total iron is similar despite lower areal density, explained by increased body size.

claim: With aging, iron redistributes in C. elegans out of the ferritin peak and accumulates in the HMW and LMW peaks.
source: With aging, iron redistributes in C. elegans out of the ferritin peak (where it is sequestered in redox-silent storage reserves) and accumulates in the HMW and LMW peaks (James et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to James et al., 2015.

claim: SIH treatment decreases iron associated with the LMW peak in aged C. elegans (10 days post adulthood).
source: The chromatographic profile of aged C. elegans (10 days post adulthood) treated with SIH (Figure 3D) revealed decreased iron associated with the LMW peak (normalized peak area approximately 40%).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SIH treatment decreases ferritin-bound iron in aged C. elegans (10 days post adulthood).
source: Ferritin-bound iron was also similarly decreased by SIH (normalized peak area approximately 50%), but iron bound within HMW species was unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SIH treatment does not affect iron bound within HMW species in aged C. elegans.
source: Ferritin-bound iron was also similarly decreased by SIH (normalized peak area approximately 50%), but iron bound within HMW species was unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Age-related changes in LMW iron are consistent with increased labile iron.
source: The age-related changes in LMW iron are consistent with increased labile iron, which is withdrawn as the substrate for ferroptosis by SIH treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the chromatography data and the known mechanism of SIH.

claim: Fe2+ in the labile iron pool is the specific substrate for ferroptosis.
source: Since Fe2+ in the labile iron pool is the specific substrate for ferroptosis, and rises with aging in C. elegans (James et al., 2015), we investigated the impact of our interventions using φXANES (James et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of ferroptosis mechanisms and is supported by citation to James et al., 2015.

claim: Fe2+ rises with aging in C. elegans.
source: Since Fe2+ in the labile iron pool is the specific substrate for ferroptosis, and rises with aging in C. elegans (James et al., 2015), we investigated the impact of our interventions using φXANES (James et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to James et al., 2015.

claim: The age-related increase in the Fe2+ fraction is normalized to that of a young animal by both Lip-1 and SIH treatments.
source: We found that the age-related increase in the Fe2+ fraction was normalized to that of a young animal by both Lip-1 and SIH treatments (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by φXANES spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Lethal glutathione depletion by DEM causes a marked increase in the Fe2+ fraction in 4 day old wild type worms.
source: φXANES of 4 day old wild type worms treated with DEM identified a marked increase in the Fe2+ fraction (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C & D; Supplementary file 3), revealing the upper limit for tolerable Fe2+ fraction being about 0.3 of the total iron (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by φXANES spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The upper limit for tolerable Fe2+ fraction is about 0.3 of the total iron.
source: φXANES of 4 day old wild type worms treated with DEM identified a marked increase in the Fe2+ fraction (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C & D; Supplementary file 3), revealing the upper limit for tolerable Fe2+ fraction being about 0.3 of the total iron (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the φXANES data showing Fe2+ fraction increases to about 0.3 under lethal DEM treatment.

claim: The observed increase in Fe2+ during normal aging is about 0.3 of the total iron.
source: These results help to contextualize the observed increase in Fe2+ during normal aging also being about 0.3 of the total iron (Figure 4C), which was normalized to ≈0.2 by Lip-1 or SIH intervention.
evidence: This claim is supported by φXANES spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lip-1 or SIH intervention normalizes the Fe2+ fraction during aging to approximately 0.2.
source: These results help to contextualize the observed increase in Fe2+ during normal aging also being about 0.3 of the total iron (Figure 4C), which was normalized to ≈0.2 by Lip-1 or SIH intervention.
evidence: This claim is supported by φXANES spectroscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment of C. elegans with Lip-1 markedly extends lifespan with an average ~70% increase in median lifespan.
source: We found that treatment of C. elegans with Lip-1 markedly extended lifespan [Figure 5A and B; average ~70% increase in median lifespan (eight independent replicates; p<0.002), Supplementary file 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Targeting the accumulation of late life iron using SIH results in a marked increase in median lifespan with an average ~100% median increase.
source: Targeting the accumulation of late life iron using SIH also resulted in a marked increase in median lifespan [Figure 5A and B; average ~100% median increase (eight independent replicates; p<0.0001), Supplementary file 4].
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Exposing C. elegans to 250 µM SIH as an iron complex (Fe(SIH)2NO3) neutralizes the benefits of SIH on lifespan.
source: Exposing C. elegans to 250 µM SIH as an iron complex (Fe(SIH)2NO3) neutralized the benefits of SIH on lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), confirming that the rescue mechanism required SIH being free to ligate iron.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The rescue mechanism of SIH requires SIH being free to ligate iron.
source: Exposing C. elegans to 250 µM SIH as an iron complex (Fe(SIH)2NO3) neutralized the benefits of SIH on lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), confirming that the rescue mechanism required SIH being free to ligate iron.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that pre-complexed SIH does not extend lifespan.

claim: Lip-1 primarily alters late life survival.
source: Treatment with Lip-1 primarily altered late life survival, while SIH extended mid-life with a squaring of the survival curve.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival curves and hazard rate analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: SIH extends mid-life with a squaring of the survival curve.
source: Treatment with Lip-1 primarily altered late life survival, while SIH extended mid-life with a squaring of the survival curve.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival curves shown in Figure 5.

claim: The lifespan increases by Lip-1 and SIH are not consistent with the temporal scaling model.
source: We found that the lifespan increases were not consistent with the temporal scaling model (p<0.01; Supplementary file 5), so the interventions may target previously unrecognized aging mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using accelerated failure time models shown in Supplementary file 5.

claim: For SIH treatment, the risk of death (hazard) in early adulthood is greatly reduced compared to control populations but rises precipitously in late life.
source: For SIH treatment, the risk of death (hazard) in early adulthood was greatly reduced compared to control populations but rose precipitously in late life (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by hazard rate analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Lip-1 markedly reduces the rate of mortality in the post-reproductive period (late-life) with early life mortality closer to that seen in untreated populations.
source: In contrast, Lip-1 markedly reduced the rate of mortality in the post-reproductive period (late-life) with early life mortality closer to that seen in untreated populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by hazard rate analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ferroptotic cell death limits lifespan in late life rather than being a global regulator of aging.
source: These findings are consistent with ferroptotic cell death limiting lifespan in late life rather than being a global regulator (e.g. insulin/IGF-1 pathway) of aging.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the non-temporal scaling effects and distinct hazard rate patterns of Lip-1 and SIH.

claim: SIH-treated animals grow substantially larger than control animals.
source: Distinctly, SIH-treated animals grew substantially larger. Following one day of treatment all animals were of similar body length (Figure 6A & B). After 4 days and 8 days of intervention, adult SIH-treated animals were significantly longer compared to similarly aged controls (e.g. control 1440 ± 123 µm versus SIH 1696 ± 64 µm, means ± SD on Day 8, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: After 4 days and 8 days of intervention, adult SIH-treated animals are significantly longer compared to similarly aged controls.
source: After 4 days and 8 days of intervention, adult SIH-treated animals were significantly longer compared to similarly aged controls (e.g. control 1440 ± 123 µm versus SIH 1696 ± 64 µm, means ± SD on Day 8, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: SIH induces an increase in body volume between Days 1 and 4.
source: In addition, SIH induced an increase in body volume between Days 1 and 4, but not thereafter (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body volume measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SIH-treated worms grow to greater volume than both control and Lip-1-treated worms at Day 4.
source: SIH-treated worms grew to greater volume than both control and Lip-1-treated worms at Day 4, indicating that preventing iron accumulation can improve animal robustness (for all comparisons see Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by body volume measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Preventing iron accumulation can improve animal robustness.
source: SIH-treated worms grew to greater volume than both control and Lip-1-treated worms at Day 4, indicating that preventing iron accumulation can improve animal robustness (for all comparisons see Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that SIH-treated animals have greater body volume.

claim: Lip-1 has no effect on body length or volume.
source: Lip-1 had no effect on length or volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by body size measurements shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Early fertility (first 24 hr) is not altered by either SIH or Lip-1 treatment.
source: Early fertility (first 24 hr) was not altered by either SIH or Lip-1 treatment (Figure 6D; p>0.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by fertility data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Lip-1 treatment results in a small decrease in lifetime reproductive output.
source: Lip-1 treatment resulted in a small decrease in lifetime reproductive output (Figure 6D; p<0.05), but SIH had no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by fertility data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SIH has no effect on lifetime reproductive output.
source: Lip-1 treatment resulted in a small decrease in lifetime reproductive output (Figure 6D; p<0.05), but SIH had no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by fertility data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Peak motile velocity correlates strongly with C. elegans healthspan and longevity.
source: The effects of both interventions on movement parameters were assessed, since peak motile velocity has been previously demonstrated to correlate strongly with C. elegans healthspan and longevity and may be considered the best estimate of healthspan (Hahm et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hahm et al., 2015.

claim: Control animals show a steady decline in maximum velocity as they age.
source: As expected, control animals showed a steady decline in maximum velocity as they aged (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by movement data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Treatment with SIH or Lip-1 markedly improves the maximum velocity of aging animals.
source: Treatment with SIH or Lip-1 markedly improved the maximum velocity of aging animals (Figure 6E), with increases also in distance travelled and mean velocity (Supplementary file 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by movement data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Combined late-life dysregulation of glutathione and iron triggers ferroptosis in C. elegans.
source: Our findings indicate that combined late-life dysregulation of glutathione and iron may trigger ferroptosis in C. elegans and that activation of this cell death signal limits lifespan.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing glutathione depletion, iron accumulation, and ferroptosis markers increase with age.

claim: Activation of ferroptosis limits lifespan in C. elegans.
source: Our findings indicate that combined late-life dysregulation of glutathione and iron may trigger ferroptosis in C. elegans and that activation of this cell death signal limits lifespan.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lifespan extension observed with ferroptosis inhibitors.

claim: As C. elegans age, intracellular iron accumulates and the capacity to safely sequester iron in ferritin fails.
source: We previously determined that as C. elegans age, not only does intracellular iron accumulate but the capacity to safely sequester iron in the iron-storage protein ferritin fails.
evidence: This claim is based on previous findings by the authors.

claim: Failure to sequester iron in ferritin contributes to the increased cellular fraction of Fe2+.
source: This contributes to the increased cellular fraction of Fe2+ that we observed here, leading to increased oxidative load (James et al., 2016; James et al., 2015), and providing the specific substrate for ferroptosis (Gaschler et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed increase in Fe2+ fraction with age and is supported by citations.

claim: The observed depletion of glutathione during aging lowers the threshold for ferroptosis.
source: The observed depletion of glutathione during aging further lowers the threshold for ferroptosis (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and is supported by citation to Dixon et al., 2012.

claim: In normal aging, a decrease in GSH couples with an age-related increase in labile Fe2+ to multiply the likelihood of ferroptosis.
source: Thus, in normal aging, a decrease in GSH couples with an age-related increase in labile Fe2+ to multiply the likelihood of ferroptosis, leading to death when combined changes in iron and GSH reach a critical threshold (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental findings on glutathione depletion and iron accumulation.

claim: SIH and Lip-1 increase lifespan by prohibiting ferroptotic death rather than inhibiting aging rate.
source: We find that SIH and Lip-1 increase lifespan by prohibiting ferroptotic death rather than inhibiting aging rate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the non-temporal scaling analysis and distinct hazard rate patterns.

claim: Late-life ferroptosis is a prominent contributor to age-related frailty.
source: We find also that late-life ferroptosis is a prominent contributor to age-related frailty.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the healthspan improvements observed with ferroptosis inhibition.

claim: Healthspan improvement need not always require a change in global aging but can result from preventing a cause of frailty.
source: The healthspan benefits of inhibiting ferroptosis confirm that healthspan improvement need not always require a change in global aging but can result from preventing a cause of frailty, raising an exciting conceptual prospect for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ferroptosis inhibition improves healthspan without temporal scaling.

claim: Iron is critical to a growing organism.
source: Iron is critical to a growing organism, yet unnecessary retention might predispose towards increased frailty later in life (Gems and Partridge, 2013; Hare et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and is supported by citations.

claim: Unnecessary iron retention might predispose towards increased frailty later in life.
source: Iron is critical to a growing organism, yet unnecessary retention might predispose towards increased frailty later in life (Gems and Partridge, 2013; Hare et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gems and Partridge, 2013 and Hare et al., 2015.

claim: Limiting iron retention post-development is not only tolerable, but improves health and life history traits.
source: This revealed that limiting iron retention post-development was not only tolerable, but improved health and life history traits.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing improved lifespan, healthspan, and body size with SIH treatment.

claim: SIH and Lip-1 act in related but different ways to extend lifespan.
source: SIH and Lip-1 alter aging at specific life phases and, unlike most known lifespan interventions, do not slow the rate of aging (Stroustrup et al., 2016). They act in related but different ways to extend lifespan, with differing impacts on hazard rate and distinct effects on iron levels, life-history traits and acute glutathione depletion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the distinct effects of SIH and Lip-1 on hazard rates, iron levels, and glutathione.

claim: Both SIH and Lip-1 increase both lifespan and healthspan without apparent major fitness trade-offs.
source: Importantly, both interventions increase both lifespan and healthspan without apparent major fitness trade-offs, in contrast to those previously reported in long-lived mutants that do slow the rate of aging (Jenkins et al., 2004; Walker et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing improved lifespan and healthspan with minimal effects on fertility.

claim: Neither SIH nor Lip-1 cause nuclear localization of DAF-16.
source: Neither SIH nor Lip-1 cause nuclear localization of DAF-16, however, we have previously shown that daf-2 mutants exhibit markedly attenuated age-related iron accumulation (James et al., 2015), so this well-studied lifespan pathway may also impact the rate of ferroptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by DAF-16::GFP localization data.

claim: daf-2 mutants exhibit markedly attenuated age-related iron accumulation.
source: Neither SIH nor Lip-1 cause nuclear localization of DAF-16, however, we have previously shown that daf-2 mutants exhibit markedly attenuated age-related iron accumulation (James et al., 2015), so this well-studied lifespan pathway may also impact the rate of ferroptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to James et al., 2015.

claim: The insulin-like signaling pathway may impact the rate of ferroptosis.
source: Neither SIH nor Lip-1 cause nuclear localization of DAF-16, however, we have previously shown that daf-2 mutants exhibit markedly attenuated age-related iron accumulation (James et al., 2015), so this well-studied lifespan pathway may also impact the rate of ferroptosis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that daf-2 mutants have reduced iron accumulation.

claim: Reduction of glutathione via RNAi treatment decreases daf-2 lifespan.
source: Interestingly, reduction of glutathione via RNAi treatment is reported to decrease daf-2 lifespan (Spanier et al., 2010), but in wild type animals has been found to cause a minor (4–7%) lifespan increase (Urban et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Spanier et al., 2010.

claim: In wild type animals, reduction of glutathione via RNAi causes a minor (4-7%) lifespan increase.
source: Interestingly, reduction of glutathione via RNAi treatment is reported to decrease daf-2 lifespan (Spanier et al., 2010), but in wild type animals has been found to cause a minor (4–7%) lifespan increase (Urban et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Urban et al., 2017.

claim: Approaches targeting iron and/or lipid peroxidation are likely to be more successful in preventing ferroptosis than approaches targeting glutathione.
source: With respect to lifespan intervention, the non-linear responses observed with glutathione reduction (Urban et al., 2017) and compensatory mechanisms (Ferguson and Bridge, 2019; Urban et al., 2017) suggest that approaches targeting iron and/or lipid peroxidation are likely to be more successful in preventing ferroptosis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the non-linear responses to glutathione reduction and the success of iron/lipid peroxidation targeting in this study.

claim: Long-lived genetic mutants of the insulin-like signaling pathway in C. elegans express a delay in somatic iron accumulation.
source: The results reported here are consistent with previous orthogonal studies where long-lived genetic mutants of the insulin-like signaling pathway in C. elegans express a delay in somatic iron accumulation (James et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to James et al., 2015.

claim: Ferritin null C. elegans mutants are short-lived and contain higher levels of pro-ferroptotic Fe2+.
source: Conversely, ferritin null C. elegans mutants, which lack the redox-silent ferritin Fe3+ storage pool, are short-lived and contain higher levels of pro-ferroptotic Fe2+ (James et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to James et al., 2016.

claim: Compound by bacteria interactions can play a significant role in C. elegans lifespan interventions.
source: A caveat for our interpretations is the possibility that the benefits of SIH or Lip-1 were mediated by changes induced in the bacterial food source. Compound by bacteria interactions can play a significant role in C. elegans lifespan interventions (Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Scott et al., 2017.

claim: Needless iron elevation in somatic tissue has been described in many organisms from Drosophila to rodents to humans, particularly in brain.
source: Needless iron elevation in somatic tissue has been described in many organisms from Drosophila to rodents to humans, particularly in brain (Massie et al., 1983; Massie et al., 1985; Ward et al., 2014) and might be a universal feature of aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies across different species.

claim: Needless iron elevation in somatic tissue might be a universal feature of aging.
source: Needless iron elevation in somatic tissue has been described in many organisms from Drosophila to rodents to humans, particularly in brain (Massie et al., 1983; Massie et al., 1985; Ward et al., 2014) and might be a universal feature of aging.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on observations across multiple species.

claim: There is no excretion mechanism for systemic iron in animals.
source: Notably, there is no excretion mechanism for systemic iron in animals (Coffey and Ganz, 2017; Muckenthaler et al., 2017), highlighting that while iron is limiting for development, there has been no evolutionary pressure to regulate its accumulation in post-reproductive life.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coffey and Ganz, 2017 and Muckenthaler et al., 2017.

claim: While iron is limiting for development, there has been no evolutionary pressure to regulate its accumulation in post-reproductive life.
source: Notably, there is no excretion mechanism for systemic iron in animals (Coffey and Ganz, 2017; Muckenthaler et al., 2017), highlighting that while iron is limiting for development, there has been no evolutionary pressure to regulate its accumulation in post-reproductive life.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of iron excretion mechanisms and evolutionary theory.

claim: Ferroptosis plays an important role in curbing cancer.
source: Ferroptosis plays an important role in kerbing cancer but becomes inappropriately activated in ischemia and neurodegeneration, where its inhibition holds therapeutic promise (Stockwell et al., 2017; Tuo et al., 2017; Viswanathan et al., 2017; Yang and Stockwell, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ferroptosis becomes inappropriately activated in ischemia and neurodegeneration, where its inhibition holds therapeutic promise.
source: Ferroptosis plays an important role in kerbing cancer but becomes inappropriately activated in ischemia and neurodegeneration, where its inhibition holds therapeutic promise (Stockwell et al., 2017; Tuo et al., 2017; Viswanathan et al., 2017; Yang and Stockwell, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The cancer-protective benefit of ferroptosis may involve the reciprocal acceleration of aging.
source: Future studies could test the hypothesis that the cancer-protective benefit of ferroptosis involves the reciprocal acceleration of aging.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis for future testing.
